summary.text: Writing the rank as \(n+\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\rfloor\), the proof bounds \(e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}\) strictly between \(1\) and \(2\) (using monotonic harmonic–log comparisons plus finite estimates for the initial cases), so each floor increment is \(1\) or \(2\). Since \(H_n-\log n\to\gamma\), telescoping gives limiting proportions \(e^\gamma-1\) and \(2-e^\gamma\), hence ratio \((e^\gamma-1)/(2-e^\gamma)\); explicit rational estimates from \(H_{615}\) show \(16/9<e^\gamma<41/23\), placing this ratio strictly between \(3.5\) and \(3.6\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
H_n=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1j\qquad(n\geq 1)
\]
be the harmonic partial sums, and let \(L_k=\log(k+1)\) for \(k\geq1\). We first express the rank in a useful form.

For fixed \(n\), exactly \(n-1\) harmonic sums precede \(H_n\), since the sequence \((H_n)\) is strictly increasing. Moreover,
\[
L_k<H_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k+1<e^{H_n}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k<e^{H_n}-1.
\]
There is no equality here: \(H_n\) is a positive rational number, and the Hermite–Lindemann theorem says that the exponential of a nonzero algebraic number is transcendental, so \(e^{H_n}\), in particular, is not an integer. Consequently the number of positive integers \(k\) for which \(L_k<H_n\) is
\[
\left\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\right\rfloor.
\]
Counting the \(n-1\) earlier harmonic sums, these logarithms, and \(H_n\) itself, the rank is therefore
\[
a(n)=n+\left\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\right\rfloor. \tag{1}
\]
This also gives \(a(1)=1+\lfloor e-1\rfloor=2\), in agreement with the stated sequence.

We will prove that for every \(n\geq1\),
\[
1<e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}<2. \tag{2}
\]
This is the main estimate.

We use throughout the elementary strict inequalities
\[
e^x>1+x\quad(x\ne0), \tag{3}
\]
and
\[
\log y<y-1\quad(y>0,\ y\ne1). \tag{4}
\]
The second follows from the first by applying (3) to \(x=\log y\): since \(e^{\log y}=y\), one obtains \(y>1+\log y\).

First we prove the lower bound in (2). For every \(n\geq1\), (4), applied to
\[
y=\frac{n+2}{n+1}=1+\frac1{n+1},
\]
gives
\[
\log(n+2)-\log(n+1)<\frac1{n+1}. \tag{5}
\]
Since \(\log2<1=H_1\), induction using \(H_{n+1}=H_n+1/(n+1)\) and (5) yields
\[
H_n>\log(n+1)\qquad(n\geq1). \tag{6}
\]
(For the base case, \(\log2<1\) is equivalent to \(2<e\), which follows at once from (3), or from the exponential series.) Hence
\[
e^{H_n}>n+1. \tag{7}
\]
Writing \(t=1/(n+1)>0\), we have by (3)
\[
e^t-1>t.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}
 &=e^{H_n}\left(e^{1/(n+1)}-1\right)\\
 &>(n+1)\frac1{n+1}=1.
\end{aligned} \tag{8}
\]
This proves the first half of (2).

For the upper bound, define
\[
F_m=H_m-\log m\qquad(m\geq1).
\]
Applying (3) to the negative number \(-1/(n+1)\) gives
\[
1-e^{-1/(n+1)}<\frac1{n+1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}
 &=e^{H_{n+1}}\left(1-e^{-1/(n+1)}\right)\\
 &<\frac{e^{H_{n+1}}}{n+1}
 =e^{H_{n+1}-\log(n+1)}. 
\end{aligned} \tag{9}
\]
We next note that \(F_m\) is strictly decreasing. Indeed, for \(m\geq1\), applying (3) to \(-1/(m+1)\), taking reciprocals, and then logarithms gives
\[
\frac1{m+1}<\log\frac{m+1}{m}
 =\log(m+1)-\log m. \tag{10}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
F_{m+1}-F_m
 =\frac1{m+1}-\bigl(\log(m+1)-\log m\bigr)<0.
\]
Thus, if \(n\geq4\), then
\[
H_{n+1}-\log(n+1)=F_{n+1}\leq F_5=H_5-\log5.
\]
Since
\[
H_5=1+\frac12+\frac13+\frac14+\frac15=\frac{137}{60},
\]
(9) gives
\[
e^{H_{n+1}}-e^{H_n}<\frac{e^{137/60}}5. \tag{11}
\]
We need only the elementary numerical estimate
\[
e^{137/60}<10. \tag{12}
\]
For completeness, this can be obtained entirely from rational bounds. The exponential series, with its positive terms and a geometric estimate for its tail, gives
\[
e<\frac{27182818286}{10^{10}}.
\]
Also, the first four terms of the exponential series give
\[
e^{43/60}\geq
\sum_{i=0}^{3}\frac{(43/60)^i}{i!}
=\frac{2637127}{1296000}.
\]
Because \(137/60=3-43/60\),
\[
e^{137/60}=\frac{e^3}{e^{43/60}}
\leq
\frac{(27182818286/10^{10})^3}{2637127/1296000}<10;
\]
the last inequality is a direct integer cross-multiplication. This proves (12), and (11) is consequently less than \(2\).

It remains to check the three indices \(n=1,2,3\), which were not covered by the comparison with \(F_5\). Here
\[
H_1=1,
\qquad H_2=\frac32,
\qquad H_3=\frac{11}{6},
\qquad H_4=\frac{25}{12}.
\]
The same exponential-series estimates give the following convenient rational bounds:
\[
e^{3/2}<\frac92,
\qquad e>\frac{27182818283}{10^{10}}, \tag{13}
\]
\[
e^{11/6}<\frac{313}{50},
\qquad e^{3/2}>\frac{447}{100}, \tag{14}
\]
and
\[
e^{25/12}<\frac{804}{100},
\qquad e^{11/6}>\frac{31}{5}. \tag{15}
\]
To see that these are again finite rational checks, one may raise both positive sides to the appropriate denominator powers. For example,
\[
(e^{3/2})^2=e^3,
\quad (e^{11/6})^6=e^{11},
\quad (e^{25/12})^{12}=e^{25},
\]
and then use
\[
\frac{27182818283}{10^{10}}<e<
\frac{27182818286}{10^{10}}.
\]
Thus the six assertions in (13)–(15) reduce respectively to direct comparisons of powers of rational numbers. Their role is simply to give
\[
e^{H_2}-e^{H_1}<\frac92-\frac{27182818283}{10^{10}}<2,
\]
\[
e^{H_3}-e^{H_2}<\frac{313}{50}-\frac{447}{100}<2,
\]
and
\[
e^{H_4}-e^{H_3}<\frac{804}{100}-\frac{31}{5}<2.
\]
Together with (8) and the argument for \(n\geq4\), this completes the proof of (2).

We now pass from (2) to the differences of ranks. We use the following simple floor observation. If \(x,y\geq0\) and
\[
1<x-y<2,
\]
then
\[
\lfloor x\rfloor-\lfloor y\rfloor\in\{1,2\}. \tag{16}
\]
Indeed, \(\lfloor x\rfloor\leq x<\lfloor x\rfloor+1\), and similarly for \(y\). These inequalities imply that the integer \(\lfloor x\rfloor-\lfloor y\rfloor\) is strictly positive and strictly less than \(3\), so it is \(1\) or \(2\).

Apply (16) with
\[
x=e^{H_{n+1}}-1,
\qquad y=e^{H_n}-1.
\]
Both are nonnegative, and (2) supplies the required difference bounds. Hence
\[
\left\lfloor e^{H_{n+1}}-1\right\rfloor-
\left\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\right\rfloor\in\{1,2\}.
\]
Using (1), we conclude that
\[
a(n+1)-a(n)
=1+\left(\left\lfloor e^{H_{n+1}}-1\right\rfloor-
\left\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\right\rfloor\right)
\in\{2,3\}. \tag{17}
\]
This proves the first part of the conjecture.

We next determine the limiting ratio of the number of \(3\)'s to the number of \(2\)'s. Let
\[
T_N=\#\{1\leq n\leq N:a(n+1)-a(n)=3\}
\]
and
\[
U_N=\#\{1\leq n\leq N:a(n+1)-a(n)=2\}.
\]
By (17), \(U_N=N-T_N\). Also every one of the \(N\) differences contributes a baseline value \(2\), and every occurrence of \(3\) contributes one additional unit. Telescoping therefore gives
\[
a(N+1)-a(1)=2N+T_N,
\]
or
\[
T_N=a(N+1)-a(1)-2N. \tag{18}
\]

Let \(\gamma\) denote the Euler–Mascheroni constant. The classical harmonic-number limit is
\[
H_n-\log n\longrightarrow\gamma. \tag{19}
\]
Exponentiating (19) and using \(e^{H_n-\log n}=e^{H_n}/n\), we obtain
\[
\frac{e^{H_n}}n\longrightarrow e^\gamma. \tag{20}
\]
For every nonnegative \(z\),
\[
z-1<\lfloor z\rfloor\leq z.
\]
Taking \(z=e^{H_n}-1\), dividing by \(n\), and using (20), the squeeze theorem yields
\[
\frac{\lfloor e^{H_n}-1\rfloor}{n}\longrightarrow e^\gamma. \tag{21}
\]
From the rank formula (1), together with \((N+1)/N\to1\), it follows that
\[
\frac{a(N+1)}N
=\frac{N+1}{N}+
\frac{\lfloor e^{H_{N+1}}-1\rfloor}{N}
\longrightarrow 1+e^\gamma. \tag{22}
\]
(The second term may be written as its quotient by \(N+1\), which tends to \(e^\gamma\), multiplied by \((N+1)/N\), which tends to \(1\).)

Divide (18) by \(N\). Since the fixed number \(a(1)\) divided by \(N\) tends to zero, (22) gives
\[
\frac{T_N}{N}\longrightarrow e^\gamma-1. \tag{23}
\]
As \(U_N=N-T_N\), we likewise obtain
\[
\frac{U_N}{N}\longrightarrow 2-e^\gamma. \tag{24}
\]
We will shortly show that \(e^\gamma<2\), so the limit in (24) is positive. It follows in particular that \(U_N>0\) for all sufficiently large \(N\), and division of (23) by (24) gives
\[
\frac{T_N}{U_N}
=\frac{T_N/N}{U_N/N}
\longrightarrow
\frac{e^\gamma-1}{2-e^\gamma}. \tag{25}
\]
Thus it remains to locate this constant between \(3.5\) and \(3.6\).

We establish the rational enclosure
\[
\frac{16}{9}<e^\gamma<\frac{41}{23}. \tag{26}
\]
Here are the details of the finite estimate used for (26). The standard integral comparison for harmonic sums gives, for every positive integer \(m\),
\[
H_m-\log(m+1)<\gamma<H_m-\log m. \tag{27}
\]
For example, (27) follows by observing that the left and right expressions are respectively increasing and decreasing to the common limit \(\gamma\), using the strict integral inequalities for the decreasing function \(1/x\).

Take \(m=615\), and put
\[
y=7-H_{615}.
\]
Exact rational summation of \(H_{615}=\sum_{j=1}^{615}1/j\) gives
\[
6<H_{615}<7,
\]
so \(0<y<1\). From (3),
\[
1-y<e^{-y}
\quad\text{and}\quad
1+y<e^y,
\]
and the latter inequality implies
\[
e^{-y}<\frac1{1+y}.
\]
Since \(H_{615}=7-y\), it follows that
\[
e^7(1-y)<e^{H_{615}}<\frac{e^7}{1+y}. \tag{28}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
e^7(H_{615}-6)<e^{H_{615}}<
\frac{e^7}{8-H_{615}}. \tag{29}
\]
Use once more the rational enclosure
\[
L:=\frac{27182818283}{10^{10}}<e<
U:=\frac{27182818286}{10^{10}}.
\]
Exact rational arithmetic with the finite rational number \(H_{615}\) gives
\[
\frac{16}{9}<\frac{L^7(H_{615}-6)}{616}, \tag{30}
\]
and
\[
\frac{U^7}{(8-H_{615})615}<\frac{41}{23}. \tag{31}
\]
These are finite integer cross-multiplications after writing \(H_{615}\) over a common denominator. Combining (29)–(31) yields
\[
\frac{16}{9}<\frac{e^{H_{615}}}{616},
\qquad
\frac{e^{H_{615}}}{615}<\frac{41}{23}. \tag{32}
\]
On the other hand, exponentiating (27) at \(m=615\) gives
\[
\frac{e^{H_{615}}}{616}<e^\gamma<
\frac{e^{H_{615}}}{615}. \tag{33}
\]
Equations (32) and (33) prove (26).

In particular, \(e^\gamma<41/23<2\), justifying the positivity used in passing to (25). Finally, the function
\[
f(x)=\frac{x-1}{2-x}
\]
is strictly increasing for \(1<x<2\), since
\[
f'(x)=\frac1{(2-x)^2}>0.
\]
At the two rational endpoints in (26),
\[
f\left(\frac{16}{9}\right)
=\frac{7/9}{2/9}=\frac72=3.5,
\]
and
\[
f\left(\frac{41}{23}\right)
=\frac{18/23}{5/23}=\frac{18}{5}=3.6.
\]
The inequalities in (26) are strict, hence
\[
3.5<\frac{e^\gamma-1}{2-e^\gamma}<3.6. \tag{34}
\]
Combining (17), (25), and (34), every successive difference is \(2\) or \(3\), and the ratio of the number of \(3\)'s to the number of \(2\)'s among the first \(N\) differences tends to the limit
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \frac{e^\gamma-1}{2-e^\gamma}},
\]
which lies strictly between \(3.5\) and \(3.6\), as required.
